full_text:
Interviewer:	Would it help if I tell you a bit about the project before we started?

Subject:	Yes, you can if you want to.

Interviewer:	OK, we’re interviewing mainly women engineering students that are going on placement. I don’t think you’re going - you’re not going are you? (No) Well we also want to interview people that aren’t going on placement to get some sort of a comparison. So we’re looking at why people chose to do engineering and at their early educational experiences and their expectations of the workplace as well. And then we’re going to go back to the placement students, while they’re on placement and find out how their expectations meet the reality. And what we’re trying to do is develop a policy document to give to the Engineering bodies to try and improve women’s retention in the industry. So that’s it in a nutshell. Is it aero you’re doing?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	What A levels did you do?

Subject:	I did physics, maths and computing and I did a business AS level as well.

Interviewer:	OK, what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	School? You mean for the ‘A’ levels?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	I went to sixth form college.

Interviewer:	OK, and have you got any previous work experience?

Subject:	Not in the engineering department, no.

Interviewer:	OK, what about your parents, what do they do? Are either of them engineers?

Subject:	No neither of my parents, my dad works for [company] but both my Grandfathers were engineers, which I learnt afterwards.

Interviewer:	So, when and how do you think you decided to do engineering?

Subject:	Er, it was kind of secondary school. I think it was just ‘cos I liked building things. I always liked taking stuff apart and building things but because, at secondary school, they were all kind of well, girls can’t build things, I thought well, I’m gonna show ‘em. So I thought right, I want to start building things, so it just kind of got on from there. But it’s completely different now I’m doing the degree ‘cos it’s more thought, rather than actually building, but yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think there’s anything particular that influenced your decision? Were your family supportive, did you have any careers advice –anything like that?

Subject:	Erm, I think that what persuaded me, ‘cos first of all I was debating about – between accountancy and engineering but I think what swayed me, that engineering is such a good basis for anything afterwards (yeah) to start off with if you’ve got an engineering degree, because that’s kind of communication, maths (yeah), physics you’ve got in there – so that’s what swayed me to – to start. So you can go wherever I want, you know.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much career research?

Subject:	Erm, I didn’t do much because I was pretty hell bent on doing engineering from secondary school. I just went on that, is it Kudos? Where it asks you questions and it comes up with what your ideal - and it came up with A levels for engineering and I thought well I’m not gonna argue with that, so…

Interviewer:	Is that the reason that you decided to do aeronautical or did you ever consider any other sort of engineering?

Subject:	Obviously there was going to be a debate between auto engineering and aero engineering. So I looked round, I was doing – I looked at mechanical engineering at other uni’s and I decided, in the end, to do aero because actually here they told me well you can start with aero, if you’re not happy with aero you can go to auto. So I started with aero and I found it quite interesting.

Interviewer:	OK, How did you decide to come to [this] University?

Subject:	Erm, I think it was when you see the AU accreditations for the course – there’s only 3 in the country. I think [university 2’s] one and I can’t remember what the third one is. And it’s only an hour away from home as well. I can go back if I want. But no, it’s –er, ‘cos I went to [university 3] and [university 2] but it just seemed the best one on the open day. They seemed to draw me in.

Interviewer:	OK, When you started out did you realise that engineering was so male dominated?

Subject:	Erm, I kind of knew that already, ‘cos from my A levels I was like I was the only girl in my class – or one of two girls that - coming here this is sort of – there’s only 7 girls on my course –oooh.

Interviewer:	Out of how many?

Subject:	I think there’s about 70 on the course. There’s 7 girls and in auto, there’s about 2 girls on there.

Interviewer:	Does that ever bother you then, that there weren’t as many women?

Subject:	No, it’s not bothered it’s just sort of – everyone’s are good for you - stand up for yourself – I sort of – I just hope more people get into it – well more women, because I know that it’s sort of well it’s male – they get to do all this, but you know, we should be able to do more of it, because we’re better than them. (laughter) We can think better than them.

Interviewer:	What do you think needs to be done to get more women involved then?

Subject:	It does need to seem a bit less male orientated. I don’t know if it’s just ‘cos engineering’s got a sort of – not like a – you know like a mechanic type, greasy type of thing, that’s what you’re gonna end up with – that’s the (?). It needs to be – come more over like actually for them to realise that it takes a lot of thinking and, at the end of the day, it’s a great thing to do because it will always stand you in good stead for the future.

Interviewer:	When you were at school were you told much about what engineering was –– did you have any careers advice suggesting engineering is an option?

Subject:	There might have been but not in engineering – they weren’t really erm enthusiastic about engineering. They were just – they tried pushing me towards teacher and something like that – and I said no, I wanted to do engineering. And I want to study physics and maths and people are like well, OK. And, like my sister does a law degree now, so mum and dad, so mum and dad say oh yes, one’s a lawyer, one’s an engineer and they go, engineer, really? You know it’s just – if it’s kind of mm, that’s the way people see it like that but…

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s because people don’t really know what engineering is?

Subject:	Er, yes. I mean I didn’t really know about it till I got here – I just thought like building stuff but the amount of thought that goes into it, and design and it’s just the whole like – thermodynamics and fluids, well…

Interviewer:	Do you think there needs to be more information generally about what engineering is maybe in schools? Would that help?

Subject:	Definitely in schools. Like secondary school, they really should include more information about engineering, definitely. I know that would have helped me I think

Interviewer:	What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Erm, open-mindedness, like sort of people’s ideas, but at the same time, stick to what you think, be able to think through it logically. You have to be able to cope with a lot of work. It’s not an easy subject. Erm, so yeah, hard working and you do get to enjoy it at the same time, so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of the characteristics are maybe more male or more female?

Subject:	I don’t know because the hard working seems to be a more female type of thing, so I don’t know. I guess males they think can think more logically and more 3D. There’s something – there’s something there that males are more spatially aware than females but I don’t think that’s true. I think we can think our ways round it a lot more than they think we can.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think there are any advantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	You can play the gender card a lot. Erm, yeah because it’s all kind of a new – you know – equality type thing, there’s more chance of a female getting a job than a male, which is kind of good but then you think hang on, have I got this job just because I’m female or have I got it for my abilities, so, but hopefully it’s just for the ability.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think are the disadvantages then?

Subject:	Erm, because it’s looked at as a male dominant thing, I think they’d rather go for males than females for things, but it’s all – I mean because like the pilots and stuff like that, it’s all a bit male pilot – women are navigators. So it’s still – there is s a difference.

Interviewer:	Ok, has your degree been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	No, I thought there’d be more building on it, but it’s opened my eyes to like loads more subjects and made me think so, well we might whinge a lot about the amount of lectures we have compared to all the other courses, they’ve all got reading week this week, and it’s then lectures, but at the end of it I know I’ll – I know I’ll be disappointed if I don’t do well so…

Interviewer:	Is the main difference that you thought there’d be more hands on, practical stuff?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	What would you say are the best and the worst things, so far, about the course?

Subject:	Oh one of the best things was last summer when we had to build a glider on the course. We all, we all whinged ‘cos we had like 2 weeks off our summer holidays at the start, but it was a fantastic 2 weeks cos we had just like the run of the uni, while we were building it and it just brought everything from the year together. And everyone’s got – it was the first time probably everyone’s been relaxed so, yeah, really enjoyed that, and worst, erm can I say exams? (yeah) So yeah, it’s just the amount of exams that we’re getting – 7 and 8 – most of the people have got like – have only got 2.

Interviewer:	Are you pleased that you have chosen this course then?

Subject:	There’s some good days and bad days but I know at the end of it I’ll be – if I get a decent mark out of it, I’ll be happy.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	Erm, [name] – one. She was our Head of Year, apart from that no. Say, well, we’ve had one but that was for just business studies (right) – a part of the course but only one.

Interviewer:	And do you notice and think whether the female lecturers treat you any differently to the male lecturers?

Subject:	No, it seems pretty much the same, I think.

Interviewer:	OK, and did any of the lecturers treat the female and male students differently, do you think?

Subject:	I think when asking questions they make sure they don’t pick on the females ‘cos then we’d say – well, there’s only 6 of us, you know, don’t keep asking us the questions, but apart from that no – it’s pretty equal I think.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s cos they’re worried about…?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Would you find it encouraging if you did have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah, I think it’d be quite – I think it would be (?) I think yeah, it would be quite nice – there is only the one female lecturer but it is well, I guess it’s to be expected, but more females because they’re nicer – yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that having a female lecturer, is like a role model – like if they can do it I can do it sort of thing or..?

Subject:	Yeah, if they can make it, yeah.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yes, but I haven’t seen them.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	Male. I’ve only seen him – I saw him for the very first time in 2 years, but I think he’s like a part time person as well, so.

Interviewer:	Would you rather have someone else as your personal tutor?

Subject:	Yeah and talk me through stuff like that. I’ve heard [female lecturer’s] a very good personal tutor -to the girls anyway.

Interviewer:	Do you think that women make better personal tutors or – or do you think it would be easier for a woman to relate to another woman or...?

Subject:	I don’t know – women are like generally better personal tutors – I don’t know whether it’s like maternal instincts, and stuff like that but – I had – my personal tutor at sixth form was female, because I was the only girl in computing and she took me for that as well, and we got quite close so I don’t know whether that was an advantage or not.

Interviewer:	Is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

Subject:	Well, there’ve been 2 really good lecturers. I guess the ad – one advantage of being female, on the course, actually, is that they know your name. It’s more personal, because er there’s [lecturer 1] who took us mainly for building and stuff like that – he’s been great and [lecturer 2] – they’re really good. [Lecturer 1]’s really – you can talk to [lecturer 1] about anything, so those 2 I think, would be the best, because I’ve hardly seen [female lecturer] but everybody’s encouraging.

Interviewer:	Yeah, have you had to do much group work?

Subject:	Yeah, we’ve done bits of group work for mainly the aircraft design module, so..

Interviewer:	When you’ve had to do group work how do you decide who to work with?

Subject:	Erm, well most of the times we’ve been put into groups (yeah) but the most recent one, the structural design project, 3 of us girls got together and decided, right, we’re gonna do this and get a good mark, so we decided to do the 3 of us. Which is quite good. But any other time we’ve been put alphabetically so far.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you prefer to work in groups, with other girls on the course or ...?

Subject:	Erm, it doesn’t really bother me because I had girls in my group last (time?) anyway, so it worked out well, but yeah, we kind of stick together, so..

Interviewer:	OK, do you think you do consciously stick together, because you are a minority?

Subject:	Yeah, I mean I don’t know if it’s like bias or something but I prefer to work with girls because I know they get the work done. I don’t mean to sound like really sexist or something but just experience - the boys will – well they’ll leave it to the girls, they’re like oh they can do it – sort of oh. So, I know it’s gonna be equally shared out.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Erm the good one as I said was the glider one – even though we came, we lost, got all beaten up though – it was still good. Bad experiences? No, I don’t think so. Everyone pretty much pulls their weight towards the end of it, so. The only thing I hate doing is presentations in front of everyone, so I just stand there, go bright red and shake. The group’s laughing at me.

Interviewer:	Do you think that group work is good in terms of when you do go out into work, the skills that you’ve gained from it?

Subject:	Oh definitely, I’d rather do group work than individual work on engineering any day. It’s just – because everyone understands different bits (yeah) you can just help each other, so definitely.

Interviewer:	OK, how have you decided not to go on placement?

Subject:	Er, it was a kind of – after – in between sixth form and uni I worked during the summer and I enjoy working so I thought – my problem is that I know if I take a year out, I won’t get back into the education side of it. I’d be too wanting to carry on, so I’m just thinking well I should get a degree over and then start working, that’s the problem.

Interviewer:	Do you think there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, I think the advantage of going on placement is that erm you’re closer to getting a job when you actually do come out of the degree. That’s one thing I’ve been thinking about and thinking oh I’m a bit – ‘cos I’ll find myself a bit in the deep end when I do come out, but for me, the disadvantage of going on placement would be to not be used to doing the degree again (yeah) and actually wanting the money.

Interviewer:	Ok, well that’s fair enough. Do you think that the way that you’re taught and the whole sort of educational experience, reflects what it’s going to be like in the industry?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know actually. I don’t think so I think it’s going to come from you, when you work in the industry, because it’ll be just you by yourself. You can’t ask someone else, what’s the answer to this? So, I think it will be different.

Interviewer:	Do you think there’s any way that that educational experience could be geared so it is more reflective of the industry?

Subject:	I think they should be, just to be able to prepare you a bit better for what to expect but I don’t know how they could do that. I don’t know if they could do like a placement day or something like that, once a week but.

Interviewer:	Have you been on any field trips or anything like that?

Subject:	I’ve been on a field trip to [name], but nothing like – you know (?) engineering, but no. I mean I went on a field trips at secondary school, to like [company] and stuff like that but not what – during here.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the more hands on, practical side of it, helps prepare you for going out into the industry?

Subject:	Yes, I think that’s to be more or less…

Interviewer:	Would you like to see more?

Subject:	Definitely yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you know what type of company you’d like to go and work for when you have finished?

Subject:	Probably a car company like [company] or [company], because it’s quite close to home. Erm, not sure why I’ll go for a plane one yet, but I’ll work on to that, because I’ve always been interested in cars so I’ve got to start off somewhere.

Interviewer:	Is there part of you that wishes you had done automotive?

Subject:	Erm, a little part of me yeah, but then I think – I think aero is seen slightly higher than auto (right) so I think well, OK, aero’s a bit better because when you say automotive industry and they say mechanic (yeah) they can’t exactly say that to aeronautical engineers so no?

Interviewer:	So you don’t think if you do decide to follow that path it will be a disadvantage at all that you’ve done aeronautic?

Subject:	I don’t think so because if I went into cars I’d be mainly doing like the aerodynamics stuff rather than the engines, which is mainly to do with planes as well.

Interviewer:	OK, what sort of things do you think will attract you to a company when you’re looking who you want to work for?

Subject:	Erm, probably location – like close to home, if I can get there (yeah). I know it sounds stupid but location – erm, job prospects I think. I want – I don’t want to just jump around from company to company, I want be able to know if I can stay there. So I’ll probably start off temporary but then go permanent, but yeah, stuff like that.

Interviewer:	And what about things like pay and training opportunities and maybe equal opportunities?

Subject:	Oh, to look at the equal opportunities yeah, I didn’t want to say pay. I didn’t want to say I’m going for the money.

Interviewer:	Why?

Subject:	 (?) sort of money wise. Yeah, training – yeah, training would be good, so yeah like opportunities afterwards. I want to find a company – I want be able to stay there, not just move around.

Interviewer:	How do you think that work will differ from being at University? You said that already about that I think in terms of like more things being by yourself…

Subject:	Yeah, there’ll be more responsibility in work but I think it will be easier than a degree, because at work you can just concentrate on the one section you’re dealing with, whereas I’m thinking of the whole thing, so I’m looking forward to working (OK). No exams!

Interviewer:	What about how you’re treated as well, do you think that will be different?

Subject:	Erm, to Uni? 

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	I guess so. Yeah. Thinking about it probably.

Interviewer:	For better or for worse?

Subject:	I don’t know. At one point you’re just coming out of the Uni, so they’ll be kind of like just a uni type – but then you’re (???) oh we have to be nice to you, like equal opportunities, so it’s gonna be different, but I hope not too different ‘cos it’s – I’m pretty sure it’s changing now.

Interviewer:	Do you think so? Ok. Are there any particular aspects of teaching or advice that you think will help you when you go out into the industry?

Subject:	Advice I don’t know – just sort of you might whinge now, but you just have to get on with it (laughter) that’s about the only advice I think.

Interviewer:	What about the actual skills do you think you will use what you’ve actually learnt?

Subject:	I hope so. Yeah, I’m pretty sure I will do, because it’s all – it’s all built into you know, like the theory and the practical stuff.

Interviewer:	OK, and what do you think will be the best and the worst things about working in the industry?

Subject:	Best things – money (laughs) Erm, just to be able to get out there and be working and be able to do it for yourself and not having someone else tell you, oh you’ve got this answer wrong and you know, stuff like that…No exams – erm the worst thing is the responsibility, if it does go wrong and you can get blamed for it. So it’s gonna be interesting, I’m looking forward to it.

Interviewer:	Ok, I think we’ve said a bit about this one as well but is there any way that you think the course or the university experience could better prepare you for going out into the workplace?

Subject:	Erm, just a week’s placement I guess. I mean, I know they tell you that you can do a year, but to me that’s just too long a time to be out the degree. A week and just like the holidays like, so just probably a week or day or something like that.

Interviewer:	Did you have any people from the industry, come and talk to you at the university or anything like that?

Subject:	We did, last year during the lectures, but that wasn’t about the industry that was Rolls Royce telling us about the engines and telling us about mini planes but nothing about work placements and stuff like that, so – we probably should do lectures about that.

Interviewer:	And have you had chance to speak to anyone that’s say been on a placement to find out about their experiences and what to expect?

Subject:	No, not really. I mean we’ve got some er 3rd year, well 3rd or 4th year systems on our course now. But because they’re doing like a different thing, basically they don’t talk much about their experiences, because it’s different to ours, so.

Interviewer:	Ok. In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

Subject:	5 years time? Erm, probably in Birmingham or London doing engineering somewhere.

Interviewer:	And do you think that you’ll stay in engineering?

Subject:	Erm, yeah. If not actually engineering – I want to be in an engineering company doing like admin or something like that – like that because engineering interests me.

Interviewer:	OK. What about in 10 years time?

Subject:	10 years time – I don’t know, I might have gone into design by then. ‘Cos I’d like drawing – I’m not good at it but I like doing the graphical drawings so I might have gone into design – like for a car or something.

Interviewer:	Do you think that career wise you’d like to become more specialised or go into management?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know. I haven’t thought about it, that far ahead. Erm, probably management – management sounds good.

Interviewer:	What do you think would be your ideal career then?

Subject:	My ideal career oh, er working for [company] and getting free cars. (laughter) 

Interviewer:	That would be nice?

Subject:	In somewhere hot, like in America somewhere.

Interviewer:	Would you like to travel?

Subject:	Erm, only to America. I’m not that big on travelling but I don’t mind America, ‘cos it’s hot.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

Subject:	Aero’s iffy, because the industry’s in a bit of up and down, like that. So I’d probably go more towards auto than aero because it just seems more stable – I mean most people buy a car, there’s no dangers of the car blowing up so probably more towards that than aero.

Interviewer:	What about once you’re in the industry, do you think that the prospects are good for developing your career?

Subject:	Erm, I hope so. I really do because I want to go far, you know, I want to become high and show them all that females can do it well, you know – we can boss ‘em.

Interviewer:	Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?

Subject:	Yeah, because as I said before, I think I’ve left it pretty open, so right till the end I can still say actually, I will do this. But yeah, ‘cos all the way through I’ve thought well, if I’m not happy with this I can change it but I seem pretty happy so…
Interviewer:	Yes, you wouldn’t do anything differently if you had to do it all again then?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Is there a part of you that’s still thinking maybe I don’t want to do engineering or…?

Subject:	Erm, that’s only on bad days when you whinge about how bad the course is and how much work you’ve got to do but at the end of it, you feel well, you go and get a little degree – an engineering degree so…

Interviewer:	OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the culture or characteristics of the industry?

Subject:	Characteristics of the industry? Erm, it’s a hard industry, tough, erm enjoyable though, once you get into it, interesting and I guess it’s like the future of it, because you’re building things that people are gonna use – is that 5 words.

Interviewer:	That’s 5 words. Do you think that the engineering culture is masculine?

Subject:	Definitely.

Interviewer:	Why do you think it is like that?

Subject:	It just does seem very towards the male perspective and male point of view. I don’t know exactly, just ‘cos I’m thinking how it is – it’s all (?) with the males so – it’s the only because I’m bitter about it that it does seem very male orientated. Like all the managers you hear about are male.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it’ll stay like that?

Subject:	I hope not because I think females are coming round to it now. Thinking well we can do this, we can do it better than thrm. I guess the whole point of the course that females can have that much of a career, ‘cos like of family and stuff but now people are thinking well, hang on, it’s my life. I want this job, I want to do well, so.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that any aspects of the culture will be problematic for you, going into the industry? Or once you’re in the industry?

Subject:	I hope not because I’m – I’ve got through sixth form being only one female, I’m used to being in a male orientated environment, so I hope not. I should be OK.

Interviewer:	OK, have you thought about things like family and that?

Subject:	God no, I’m only 19!

Interviewer:	Have you thought like that it might be a problem? (lost words)

Subject:	I hope it won’t be a problem. Thinking about it I don’t know. Now, I’ve got to go and find a husband that doesn’t mind being at home with the children. I’ll bring the money in, you can look after the kids.

Interviewer:	Do you think that your educational experiences differ from other students like in Social Sciences or business studies or..?

Subject:	Yeah, my best mate’s actually doing Social Sciences and they just get a couple of essays and they whinge about that and I’m sort of hold on, I go to lectures, I get to learn all this lot all the time, so I think well my course is harder.

Interviewer:	Dou think that will helps you, in some ways, when you get into the workplace?

Subject:	Yeah, ‘cos you’re used to hard slog. I mean you kind of – engineers kind of look down on the Social Sciences – arty people – sort of – oh, you’ve got an art degree? I know it’s bad but it’s just – I think it’s cos the amount of work we put into our degree, compared to how much they put into theirs – so yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s all the questions I have to ask you – thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer

turns.text: Er, it was kind of secondary school. I think it was just ‘cos I liked building things. I always liked taking stuff apart and building things but because, at secondary school, they were all kind of well, girls can’t build things, I thought well, I’m gonna show ‘em. So I thought right, I want to start building things, so it just kind of got on from there. But it’s completely different now I’m doing the degree ‘cos it’s more thought, rather than actually building, but yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think there’s anything particular that influenced your decision? Were your family supportive, did you have any careers advice –anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think that what persuaded me, ‘cos first of all I was debating about – between accountancy and engineering but I think what swayed me, that engineering is such a good basis for anything afterwards (yeah) to start off with if you’ve got an engineering degree, because that’s kind of communication, maths (yeah), physics you’ve got in there – so that’s what swayed me to – to start. So you can go wherever I want, you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you do much career research?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I didn’t do much because I was pretty hell bent on doing engineering from secondary school. I just went on that, is it Kudos? Where it asks you questions and it comes up with what your ideal - and it came up with A levels for engineering and I thought well I’m not gonna argue with that, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that the reason that you decided to do aeronautical or did you ever consider any other sort of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Obviously there was going to be a debate between auto engineering and aero engineering. So I looked round, I was doing – I looked at mechanical engineering at other uni’s and I decided, in the end, to do aero because actually here they told me well you can start with aero, if you’re not happy with aero you can go to auto. So I started with aero and I found it quite interesting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, How did you decide to come to [this] University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think it was when you see the AU accreditations for the course – there’s only 3 in the country. I think [university 2’s] one and I can’t remember what the third one is. And it’s only an hour away from home as well. I can go back if I want. But no, it’s –er, ‘cos I went to [university 3] and [university 2] but it just seemed the best one on the open day. They seemed to draw me in.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, When you started out did you realise that engineering was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I kind of knew that already, ‘cos from my A levels I was like I was the only girl in my class – or one of two girls that - coming here this is sort of – there’s only 7 girls on my course –oooh.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Out of how many?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think there’s about 70 on the course. There’s 7 girls and in auto, there’s about 2 girls on there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that ever bother you then, that there weren’t as many women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, it’s not bothered it’s just sort of – everyone’s are good for you - stand up for yourself – I sort of – I just hope more people get into it – well more women, because I know that it’s sort of well it’s male – they get to do all this, but you know, we should be able to do more of it, because we’re better than them. (laughter) We can think better than them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think needs to be done to get more women involved then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It does need to seem a bit less male orientated. I don’t know if it’s just ‘cos engineering’s got a sort of – not like a – you know like a mechanic type, greasy type of thing, that’s what you’re gonna end up with – that’s the (?). It needs to be – come more over like actually for them to realise that it takes a lot of thinking and, at the end of the day, it’s a great thing to do because it will always stand you in good stead for the future.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you were at school were you told much about what engineering was –– did you have any careers advice suggesting engineering is an option?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There might have been but not in engineering – they weren’t really erm enthusiastic about engineering. They were just – they tried pushing me towards teacher and something like that – and I said no, I wanted to do engineering. And I want to study physics and maths and people are like well, OK. And, like my sister does a law degree now, so mum and dad, so mum and dad say oh yes, one’s a lawyer, one’s an engineer and they go, engineer, really? You know it’s just – if it’s kind of mm, that’s the way people see it like that but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s because people don’t really know what engineering is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yes. I mean I didn’t really know about it till I got here – I just thought like building stuff but the amount of thought that goes into it, and design and it’s just the whole like – thermodynamics and fluids, well…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there needs to be more information generally about what engineering is maybe in schools? Would that help?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely in schools. Like secondary school, they really should include more information about engineering, definitely. I know that would have helped me I think

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, open-mindedness, like sort of people’s ideas, but at the same time, stick to what you think, be able to think through it logically. You have to be able to cope with a lot of work. It’s not an easy subject. Erm, so yeah, hard working and you do get to enjoy it at the same time, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of the characteristics are maybe more male or more female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know because the hard working seems to be a more female type of thing, so I don’t know. I guess males they think can think more logically and more 3D. There’s something – there’s something there that males are more spatially aware than females but I don’t think that’s true. I think we can think our ways round it a lot more than they think we can.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think there are any advantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You can play the gender card a lot. Erm, yeah because it’s all kind of a new – you know – equality type thing, there’s more chance of a female getting a job than a male, which is kind of good but then you think hang on, have I got this job just because I’m female or have I got it for my abilities, so, but hopefully it’s just for the ability.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think are the disadvantages then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, because it’s looked at as a male dominant thing, I think they’d rather go for males than females for things, but it’s all – I mean because like the pilots and stuff like that, it’s all a bit male pilot – women are navigators. So it’s still – there is s a difference.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, has your degree been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I thought there’d be more building on it, but it’s opened my eyes to like loads more subjects and made me think so, well we might whinge a lot about the amount of lectures we have compared to all the other courses, they’ve all got reading week this week, and it’s then lectures, but at the end of it I know I’ll – I know I’ll be disappointed if I don’t do well so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is the main difference that you thought there’d be more hands on, practical stuff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you say are the best and the worst things, so far, about the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh one of the best things was last summer when we had to build a glider on the course. We all, we all whinged ‘cos we had like 2 weeks off our summer holidays at the start, but it was a fantastic 2 weeks cos we had just like the run of the uni, while we were building it and it just brought everything from the year together. And everyone’s got – it was the first time probably everyone’s been relaxed so, yeah, really enjoyed that, and worst, erm can I say exams? (yeah) So yeah, it’s just the amount of exams that we’re getting – 7 and 8 – most of the people have got like – have only got 2.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you pleased that you have chosen this course then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There’s some good days and bad days but I know at the end of it I’ll be – if I get a decent mark out of it, I’ll be happy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, [name] – one. She was our Head of Year, apart from that no. Say, well, we’ve had one but that was for just business studies (right) – a part of the course but only one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do you notice and think whether the female lecturers treat you any differently to the male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, it seems pretty much the same, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and did any of the lecturers treat the female and male students differently, do you think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think when asking questions they make sure they don’t pick on the females ‘cos then we’d say – well, there’s only 6 of us, you know, don’t keep asking us the questions, but apart from that no – it’s pretty equal I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s cos they’re worried about…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you find it encouraging if you did have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think it’d be quite – I think it would be (?) I think yeah, it would be quite nice – there is only the one female lecturer but it is well, I guess it’s to be expected, but more females because they’re nicer – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that having a female lecturer, is like a role model – like if they can do it I can do it sort of thing or..?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, if they can make it, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, but I haven’t seen them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male. I’ve only seen him – I saw him for the very first time in 2 years, but I think he’s like a part time person as well, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you rather have someone else as your personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah and talk me through stuff like that. I’ve heard [female lecturer’s] a very good personal tutor -to the girls anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that women make better personal tutors or – or do you think it would be easier for a woman to relate to another woman or...?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know – women are like generally better personal tutors – I don’t know whether it’s like maternal instincts, and stuff like that but – I had – my personal tutor at sixth form was female, because I was the only girl in computing and she took me for that as well, and we got quite close so I don’t know whether that was an advantage or not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, there’ve been 2 really good lecturers. I guess the ad – one advantage of being female, on the course, actually, is that they know your name. It’s more personal, because er there’s [lecturer 1] who took us mainly for building and stuff like that – he’s been great and [lecturer 2] – they’re really good. [Lecturer 1]’s really – you can talk to [lecturer 1] about anything, so those 2 I think, would be the best, because I’ve hardly seen [female lecturer] but everybody’s encouraging.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, have you had to do much group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, we’ve done bits of group work for mainly the aircraft design module, so..

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you’ve had to do group work how do you decide who to work with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well most of the times we’ve been put into groups (yeah) but the most recent one, the structural design project, 3 of us girls got together and decided, right, we’re gonna do this and get a good mark, so we decided to do the 3 of us. Which is quite good. But any other time we’ve been put alphabetically so far.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you prefer to work in groups, with other girls on the course or ...?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it doesn’t really bother me because I had girls in my group last (time?) anyway, so it worked out well, but yeah, we kind of stick together, so..

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think you do consciously stick together, because you are a minority?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I mean I don’t know if it’s like bias or something but I prefer to work with girls because I know they get the work done. I don’t mean to sound like really sexist or something but just experience - the boys will – well they’ll leave it to the girls, they’re like oh they can do it – sort of oh. So, I know it’s gonna be equally shared out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm the good one as I said was the glider one – even though we came, we lost, got all beaten up though – it was still good. Bad experiences? No, I don’t think so. Everyone pretty much pulls their weight towards the end of it, so. The only thing I hate doing is presentations in front of everyone, so I just stand there, go bright red and shake. The group’s laughing at me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that group work is good in terms of when you do go out into work, the skills that you’ve gained from it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh definitely, I’d rather do group work than individual work on engineering any day. It’s just – because everyone understands different bits (yeah) you can just help each other, so definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how have you decided not to go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it was a kind of – after – in between sixth form and uni I worked during the summer and I enjoy working so I thought – my problem is that I know if I take a year out, I won’t get back into the education side of it. I’d be too wanting to carry on, so I’m just thinking well I should get a degree over and then start working, that’s the problem.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think the advantage of going on placement is that erm you’re closer to getting a job when you actually do come out of the degree. That’s one thing I’ve been thinking about and thinking oh I’m a bit – ‘cos I’ll find myself a bit in the deep end when I do come out, but for me, the disadvantage of going on placement would be to not be used to doing the degree again (yeah) and actually wanting the money.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, well that’s fair enough. Do you think that the way that you’re taught and the whole sort of educational experience, reflects what it’s going to be like in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know actually. I don’t think so I think it’s going to come from you, when you work in the industry, because it’ll be just you by yourself. You can’t ask someone else, what’s the answer to this? So, I think it will be different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there’s any way that that educational experience could be geared so it is more reflective of the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think they should be, just to be able to prepare you a bit better for what to expect but I don’t know how they could do that. I don’t know if they could do like a placement day or something like that, once a week but.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you been on any field trips or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve been on a field trip to [name], but nothing like – you know (?) engineering, but no. I mean I went on a field trips at secondary school, to like [company] and stuff like that but not what – during here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the more hands on, practical side of it, helps prepare you for going out into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think that’s to be more or less…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you like to see more?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know what type of company you’d like to go and work for when you have finished?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably a car company like [company] or [company], because it’s quite close to home. Erm, not sure why I’ll go for a plane one yet, but I’ll work on to that, because I’ve always been interested in cars so I’ve got to start off somewhere.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there part of you that wishes you had done automotive?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, a little part of me yeah, but then I think – I think aero is seen slightly higher than auto (right) so I think well, OK, aero’s a bit better because when you say automotive industry and they say mechanic (yeah) they can’t exactly say that to aeronautical engineers so no?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you don’t think if you do decide to follow that path it will be a disadvantage at all that you’ve done aeronautic?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think so because if I went into cars I’d be mainly doing like the aerodynamics stuff rather than the engines, which is mainly to do with planes as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what sort of things do you think will attract you to a company when you’re looking who you want to work for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably location – like close to home, if I can get there (yeah). I know it sounds stupid but location – erm, job prospects I think. I want – I don’t want to just jump around from company to company, I want be able to know if I can stay there. So I’ll probably start off temporary but then go permanent, but yeah, stuff like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what about things like pay and training opportunities and maybe equal opportunities?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, to look at the equal opportunities yeah, I didn’t want to say pay. I didn’t want to say I’m going for the money.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (?) sort of money wise. Yeah, training – yeah, training would be good, so yeah like opportunities afterwards. I want to find a company – I want be able to stay there, not just move around.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you think that work will differ from being at University? You said that already about that I think in terms of like more things being by yourself…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, there’ll be more responsibility in work but I think it will be easier than a degree, because at work you can just concentrate on the one section you’re dealing with, whereas I’m thinking of the whole thing, so I’m looking forward to working (OK). No exams!

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about how you’re treated as well, do you think that will be different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, to Uni?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I guess so. Yeah. Thinking about it probably.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: For better or for worse?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. At one point you’re just coming out of the Uni, so they’ll be kind of like just a uni type – but then you’re (???) oh we have to be nice to you, like equal opportunities, so it’s gonna be different, but I hope not too different ‘cos it’s – I’m pretty sure it’s changing now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think so? Ok. Are there any particular aspects of teaching or advice that you think will help you when you go out into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Advice I don’t know – just sort of you might whinge now, but you just have to get on with it (laughter) that’s about the only advice I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about the actual skills do you think you will use what you’ve actually learnt?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope so. Yeah, I’m pretty sure I will do, because it’s all – it’s all built into you know, like the theory and the practical stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what do you think will be the best and the worst things about working in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Best things – money (laughs) Erm, just to be able to get out there and be working and be able to do it for yourself and not having someone else tell you, oh you’ve got this answer wrong and you know, stuff like that…No exams – erm the worst thing is the responsibility, if it does go wrong and you can get blamed for it. So it’s gonna be interesting, I’m looking forward to it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, I think we’ve said a bit about this one as well but is there any way that you think the course or the university experience could better prepare you for going out into the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, just a week’s placement I guess. I mean, I know they tell you that you can do a year, but to me that’s just too long a time to be out the degree. A week and just like the holidays like, so just probably a week or day or something like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have any people from the industry, come and talk to you at the university or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We did, last year during the lectures, but that wasn’t about the industry that was Rolls Royce telling us about the engines and telling us about mini planes but nothing about work placements and stuff like that, so – we probably should do lectures about that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And have you had chance to speak to anyone that’s say been on a placement to find out about their experiences and what to expect?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really. I mean we’ve got some er 3rd year, well 3rd or 4th year systems on our course now. But because they’re doing like a different thing, basically they don’t talk much about their experiences, because it’s different to ours, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: 5 years time? Erm, probably in Birmingham or London doing engineering somewhere.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do you think that you’ll stay in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah. If not actually engineering – I want to be in an engineering company doing like admin or something like that – like that because engineering interests me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What about in 10 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: 10 years time – I don’t know, I might have gone into design by then. ‘Cos I’d like drawing – I’m not good at it but I like doing the graphical drawings so I might have gone into design – like for a car or something.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that career wise you’d like to become more specialised or go into management?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know. I haven’t thought about it, that far ahead. Erm, probably management – management sounds good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think would be your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My ideal career oh, er working for [company] and getting free cars. (laughter)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That would be nice?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In somewhere hot, like in America somewhere.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you like to travel?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, only to America. I’m not that big on travelling but I don’t mind America, ‘cos it’s hot.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Aero’s iffy, because the industry’s in a bit of up and down, like that. So I’d probably go more towards auto than aero because it just seems more stable – I mean most people buy a car, there’s no dangers of the car blowing up so probably more towards that than aero.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about once you’re in the industry, do you think that the prospects are good for developing your career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I hope so. I really do because I want to go far, you know, I want to become high and show them all that females can do it well, you know – we can boss ‘em.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because as I said before, I think I’ve left it pretty open, so right till the end I can still say actually, I will do this. But yeah, ‘cos all the way through I’ve thought well, if I’m not happy with this I can change it but I seem pretty happy so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, you wouldn’t do anything differently if you had to do it all again then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there a part of you that’s still thinking maybe I don’t want to do engineering or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, that’s only on bad days when you whinge about how bad the course is and how much work you’ve got to do but at the end of it, you feel well, you go and get a little degree – an engineering degree so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the culture or characteristics of the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Characteristics of the industry? Erm, it’s a hard industry, tough, erm enjoyable though, once you get into it, interesting and I guess it’s like the future of it, because you’re building things that people are gonna use – is that 5 words.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s 5 words. Do you think that the engineering culture is masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think it is like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It just does seem very towards the male perspective and male point of view. I don’t know exactly, just ‘cos I’m thinking how it is – it’s all (?) with the males so – it’s the only because I’m bitter about it that it does seem very male orientated. Like all the managers you hear about are male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it’ll stay like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope not because I think females are coming round to it now. Thinking well we can do this, we can do it better than thrm. I guess the whole point of the course that females can have that much of a career, ‘cos like of family and stuff but now people are thinking well, hang on, it’s my life. I want this job, I want to do well, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that any aspects of the culture will be problematic for you, going into the industry? Or once you’re in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope not because I’m – I’ve got through sixth form being only one female, I’m used to being in a male orientated environment, so I hope not. I should be OK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you thought about things like family and that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: God no, I’m only 19!

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you thought like that it might be a problem? (lost words)

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope it won’t be a problem. Thinking about it I don’t know. Now, I’ve got to go and find a husband that doesn’t mind being at home with the children. I’ll bring the money in, you can look after the kids.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that your educational experiences differ from other students like in Social Sciences or business studies or..?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, my best mate’s actually doing Social Sciences and they just get a couple of essays and they whinge about that and I’m sort of hold on, I go to lectures, I get to learn all this lot all the time, so I think well my course is harder.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Dou think that will helps you, in some ways, when you get into the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, ‘cos you’re used to hard slog. I mean you kind of – engineers kind of look down on the Social Sciences – arty people – sort of – oh, you’ve got an art degree? I know it’s bad but it’s just – I think it’s cos the amount of work we put into our degree, compared to how much they put into theirs – so yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s all the questions I have to ask you – thank you very much.
